lignes.texte: The video game industry is being massacred.
From 2022 to 2026, over 58,000 people were laid off. It was thought to be a 'post-COVID slump'.
A market correction. Even the effects of the burgeoning AI race was blamed.
None of that is true.
Studios aren’t collapsing because people aren’t playing games. It’s
the result of a multi-million dollar gamble by AAA publishers.
One that didn’t pay off.
And now it’s burning the gaming world to the ground.
AAA games - the high-budget, high-profile titles - always came with a hefty price
tag. Exact budgets were always kept under wraps. But industry insiders
say today’s AAA games cost more than $300 million to develop and release.
That’s more than the cost of the Harry Potter movies and most Marvel movies.
And those costs come with consequences.
Job losses.
2025 saw almost 9,200 layoffs. And 2026 is on track to be even more brutal. An industry
jobs tracker, ASGC, initially forecasted around 8,000 cuts in January. By late July,
the projection kept ticking upwards, hitting at a projection of nearly 14,000 job cuts.
And the year’s not over yet.
With budgets spiraling out of control, it’s not a surprising development. The
horrifying state of the video game industry was laid bare when hackers breached Insomniac,
the developer behind the Spider-Man 2 game.
They found that the game ran $30 million over its original budget of $270 million. It gave
the public a shocking, behind the scenes look at industry spending. Sony needed to find a way to
cut back on skyrocketing costs. The leaked files show that they requested Insomniac
“remove 50-75 people strategically”, mostly from the Wolverine and Spider-Man 3 teams.
Sony called for layoffs across pretty much all its first-party studios,
including PlayStation Studios, Destiny developer Bungie, and Naughty Dog,
the development company behind The Last of Us.
But Xbox has had it worse.
In July 2026, it announced that it would cut 3,200 jobs and divest 5 studios. Xbox CEO Asha
Sharma stated it was a necessary move because “our business today is not healthy. We are
operating at margins that are 3-10x lower than comparable platform and publishing businesses.”
She didn’t mention the disappointing sales of games like Avowed, which failed to live up to
its developer’s promises. It was happening all across the industry. Companies behind
wildly successful games - like The Last of Us - were hemorrhaging jobs and money.
Spider-Man 2, with a cost of $300 million, would need to sell 7.2 million units to
break even. Luckily, it was a success and sold 5 million units in its first 1 days on the market,
eventually making its money back and turning a profit.
But reporters have gotten hold of some other development costs that make it
clear that Spider-Man 2’s immense budget was not a fluke. The Last Of Us Part 2 cost $220
million to make. Horizon Forbidden West racked up $212 million in development
costs. The latest Call of Duty has already cost $300 million, while the much anticipated Grand
Theft Auto 6 takes the cake with an enormous estimated budget between $1 and $1.5 Billion.
But much more affordable games have seen massive critical and commercial success,
proving you don’t need sky high budgets to score a hit. Assassin’s Creed Shadows cost
Ubisoft just over $100 million. Resident Evil Requiem cost even less than that.
But AAA game developers aren’t learning the right lessons.
Or they don’t care.
Sending budgets have exploded in hopes of creating the next hit. The average AAA budget
has ballooned from between $50 and $150 million in the late 2010s, to $200-300 million in 2024.
That doesn’t include marketing costs.
According to IGN, “when considering marketing costs, this number can jump
to over $1 billion across a franchise… one large studio [reported] that a major
franchise’s development cost $660 million and marketing cost nearly $550 million.”
So when a AAA game flops, companies can quickly start to sink. Even if
they’re as massive and legendary as Warner Bros.
“Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League” was a highly problematic title before it ever hit the
market. The development of the game experienced constant delays. It was slated for debut in 2022,
but didn’t get released until 2024. It wasn’t helped by an unclear and changing vision at
the helm, and a rigid work culture stressed everyone out without delivering much of anything.
The game debuted in February 2024. By May, the writing was already on the wall.
Metacritic’s score had firmly held at a “mixed” 60, sales were flatlining,
and there was no hype in sight. On May 9th, the devastating news was shared an earnings call:
Warner Bros would be taking a $200 million loss from the Suicide Squad sequel.
It quickly became known as one of the biggest flops in gaming. To take a $200 million loss,
how much had Warner Bros. actually spent on the game? To preserve some secrecy,
or just due to embarrassment, the studio never revealed the cost of the game.
So, why do developers think they can get away with high-budget, mediocre games in the first place?
Because of shady marketing.
When companies invest hundreds of millions into a game with a multi-year development cycle,
they’re basing it on massive sales projections. When the game comes around,
they’ll do anything to make those sales happen.
Even if it means lying.
Like with Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League. Early trailers promised a cinematic,
character-heavy experience. What did fans get instead? A generic looter shooter.
Every member of the Suicide Squad was using guns instead of their character’s weapons of choice.
As one games writer put it, “people’s first reactions to
the teaser were a huge contrast to its reception on release.”
Fans were also primed to expect a usual Rocksteady debut; and were instead surprised with a live
service game. To understand why this annoyed gamers, live service games have gotten a very
bad rap. They’re known to deliver a very basic, or glitchy, or underwhelming first impression and
use constant updates or changes to keep players coming back for more. Often pressuring players
to use microtransactions in the meantime, if they want to make reasonable progress.
Not all live service games have to be that way. The bar is so low that
bucking the trend could lead to one of the most successful games of all time.
Underwhelming live service games have gotten so bad that a relatively recent
release - Concord in 2024 - easily became one of the most shocking failures of all time. The
video game cost at least $400 million to develop. Yet, when it was released,
it flopped so badly that Sony didn’t even try to save it. Instead, it removed the
game from its store after just 2 weeks and refunded every person who had bought it.
In the case of Suicide Squad, the decision to make the game a live service one, either because it was
trending or because Rocksteady wanted a cashgrab, went down like a rock. As one Reddit user put it:
“Rocksteady made fantastic single player games. No one wanted a live service Suicide Squad game.”
But even with all these issues, developers would
rely on misleading expectations and marketing to boost their game’s sales.
When Mass Effect 3 debuted in 2012, the developer had promised that each
fan would get a different ending based on their decisions throughout the story. Not just an A,
B or C choice; an actual customized ending.
Players got a generic A, B, or C ending.
Sales of Mass Effect 3 dropped by around 80% from week one to week two. Despite that, Mass Effect 3
was still a commercial success. It’s sold almost 4 million copies to date and made EA tons of money.
How? Because of a crazy amount of pre-orders. Almost one million of those copies sold on day
one. By the time people figured out the promises about the ending weren’t real,
most copies of the game had already been sold.
But Suicide Squad didn’t have that luxury.
Something had changed in the gaming world when it was released.
Specifically, on Steam.
There was a new user review UI that worked like a financial kill-switch. In 2013,
Valve had announced a new review feature for Steam users; one that quickly moved from beta testing to
the wider public. Initially conceived to give gamers a way to voice their opinions, Steam's
reviews became so influential that they determined whether a game would live or die on the market.
A single “mixed” review score could instantly vaporize a
$200 million investment. That’s exactly what happened with Suicide Squad, and many others.
All the glossy marketing in the world couldn’t cover up what actual gamer reviews on Steam:
It just wasn’t worth it.
Statistics show exactly to what degree Steam’s rating system has a hold over
the gaming world. A ‘Mixed' rating on Steam correlates with a conversion
rate approximately 60-67% lower than a 'Very Positive' rating.
Steam users generally see ratings as they’re actively browsing to buy a game.
And they pay a lot of attention to other users’ opinions. How much? GameDiscoverCo
conducted a survey to see how reviews would influence Steam users’ choices.
They found that 40.5% of respondents always check
reviews before buying. Another 32% said they did it most of the time.
That’s almost three quarters of Steam users paying close attention to reviews.
Understandably, developers are now racing to provide updates that can move the needle on a
Steam review score. Anything to make the game more attractive to the average Steam customer.
Because the payoff can be huge.
Gamesight found that using updates to change overall game reviews
“from ‘Mixed’ to ‘Very Positive’ nearly tripled conversion rates”.
In fact, Steam user reviews have become so important, they matter more than professional
critics’ opinions. They’re just a financial kill switch; but a democratic one as well.
This became obvious with Ubisoft’s Star Wars Outlaws release in 2024. With an estimated
$200 million budget, the game debuted to general critical acclaim. On Metacritic,
it received a score of 76 based on professional critic reviews. But user reviews weren’t as kind;
gamers only gave it a 4.9 out of 10 near its release date.
Steam users felt the same way.
Though several updates and bug fixes have moved Star Wars Outlaw up to “Mostly Positive”
since mid-2026, the year of its debut, the game sat firmly in the “Mixed” category.
Physical launch sales in the UK were 55% lower than the Star Wars game released a
year before that: Star Wars: Jedi Survivor. The game ended up selling only 1-2 million lifetime
units. Since Ubisoft had publicly said it would need to sell at least 3-4 million
copies of the game to break even, the market outlook on the company crashed and burned.
After the game’s release, Ubisoft’s stocks dropped by more than 10% in 2
days. Basically a market run on a video game developer. They fell to around $18 per share,
the lowest the share had ever been since 2014.
And they continued to fall.
It proved that even a critically successful game
based on a massively popular franchise like Star Wars can absolutely flop due
to Steam user reviews. It created more problems for mega-budget AAA franchises.
Xbox’s ‘Avowed’ fell prey to a similar fate.
The game’s estimated budget was between $100 -150 million. Obsidian and Microsoft
set up the game as a “spiritual successor to ‘Pillars of Eternity’”. The hype was
real. Gamers everywhere expected something amazing; a game with depth and promise.
They didn’t get it.
The game debuted to very disappointing user reviews. It received a “mixed” rating on Steam,
due to “significant technical issues, scaled-down scope compared to promises,
repetitive combat, and shallow exploration”.
Xbox even used its day-one Game Pass availability to heavily boost player engagement,
reporting 5 million players on ‘Avowed’ in its first month. But all the boosts and marketing
tactics in the world couldn’t save ‘Avowed’ after Steam users had already destroyed it.
The game tanked.
Then Microsoft announced thousands of job layoffs.
Steam may have thought its user rating system would help gamers take back some power from
critics. But Steam’s UI did much more than that. Gamers ended up taking the power back
from developers and studios as well. They were able to portray the gameplay experience as it
actually was in order to tell others users the truth. They disrupted the marketing
tactics most developers employed to hide mediocre, messy, or underdelivering games.
This made Steam users gravitate even more towards the rating system. Steam itself
also stepped in with an updated UI to encourage more reviews. This led to a
clearer public verdict on what users actually thought of games, and much more engagement.
And it would rock the gaming market.
In 2019, Steam introduced its first of many changes to get more game reviews.
Users would receive a prompt to review the game they were playing after a set number
of hours of gameplay. This was followed by sale strategies which gave users awards for
leaving reviews. Steam then began to prioritize reviews written in the user’s own language.
What this did was shatter the formula of the gaming industry.
It’s called the Boxleiter number.
In 2018, it was a reliable way to estimate a game's sales figure based entirely on
its Steam reviews. Back then, the math was simple. For every single review on its page,
you could assume a game had sold 75-80 copies. Publishers used this
metric for years to project and justify their massive budgets.
But then the calculation collapsed.
Reviews began flooding in. Journalists and industry insiders who tried to track sales
found that instead of selling around 80 games per review, the new number had plummeted to
15. Steam is allowing gamers to dictate the success or failure of any one video
game. The Boxleiter ratio shift means the 'silent majority' has found its voice.
And it is screaming.
After years of misleading marketing, endless delays, and broken promises,
gamers have found a system by them, for them, that works almost exclusively for them.
Not only are mediocre games being punished for their low quality,
but engaging games that may have flown under the radar are being propelled to success via Steam.
As the developers of one game found out
When Helldivers 2 was released, no one expected it to be the next big thing. Its success was
such a surprise that the number of users flooding onto the system crashed the server.
Developer Arrowhead publicly asked players to postpone buying the game,
so the servers could handle the unexpected capacity.
But the game was too good to pass up.
Demand exploded, with the game selling 12 million units around the world. 15 million
unique players logged in to check it out. As Arrowhead CEO Johan Pilestedt put it:
“it’s crazy to think that there are more Helldivers than there are Swedes.”
Helldivers 2 also benefited from incredible word of mouth and user ratings. Gamers were excited to
play a live service game that lived up to its promises. It offered a stable, fully-formed,
complex world right at the beginning, instead of relying on future updates. That’s how a game
that barely spent anything on marketing ended up absolutely dominating the gaming charts. And
considering the low marketing cost, Helldivers 2 achieved a significantly higher marketing return
of investment than major 2023 AAA releases like Starfield and Modern Warfare III.
The fact that Helldivers 2 had a relatively affordable price tag helps. The game only cost
$40 to buy. Most AAA games now hover in the $70 range instead. Compared to high-profile,
super-high-budget games, Helldivers 2 found itself in a David vs. Goliath scenario. Except
the slingshot cost $40 and the giant spent $200M on armor that didn't work.
It was all because Helldiers 2 focused on delivering quality,
affordable products that users loved and would talk about online…
Especially on Steam.
Eventually, Helldivers 2 was tweaked to handle its huge base of customers. It was so popular
that at times, nearly 500,000 players were simultaneously playing it on Steam.
According to one source, “it’s reasonable to estimate that Helldivers 2 has grossed
more than a billion - perhaps even more than $2 billion - by the end of 2025”.
But the secret behind Helldivers 2’ success also ended up being its - temporary - undoing.
In spring of 2024, Sony made a baffling decision. It stated PC players would
have to link a pre-existing PSN account with Steam to continue playing the game.
This was a major problem. Particularly for players in the over 100 countries where PSN
isn’t even supported. Cutting off the majority of your game’s international base wasn’t a smart
move. And gamers almost immediately used the Steam user review system to let the
developers know that. In just one weekend, Steam users flooded the game with negative reviews.
The game got delisted in over 150 countries.
Almost immediately, Sony reversed course.
Within a week, the entertainment giant announced that it’s “still
learning what is best for PC players”, and is therefore cancelling the PSN link requirement.
All in all, the developers took the review bombing in good stride and actually used
it to learn from customer feedback. They eventually created a “review bomb cape” for
the game. Its design features the user review score graph from Steam itself.
Users also got a win, in that they stopped something exclusionary from
happening to a game they love. Once again, they saw that their voices
were respected and actually listened to when they left reviews on Steam.
It’s no wonder Steam has changed the video game landscape entirely. Overpriced, bloated,
poorly conceived and designed AAA titles can’t rely on the deep pockets anymore. Publishers can’t
use shiny marketing gloss over a bad to mediocre product. But for well-intentioned developers,
the review system is a lifeline. They can use player feedback to learn from their mistakes and
fix their games in real time. And when they get it right, Steam users will let the world know.
But with the positive comes the negative.
AAA gaming was already collapsing. Tens of thousands of workers are being laid off as
major developers tightened their belts. Given this brutal reality,
the new influx of Steam reviews and vocal users might just change the landscape forever.
It’s the final spark.
And it’s setting the AAA gaming industry on fire.
Gaming studios are doing everything they can to maximize their profits. And sometimes,
it backfires completely. Watch “Ubisoft Bet On AI Slop. Now
They Are RUINED” to see how wrong they can get it. Or click on this.
